items.body:
Olivia Chow was re-elected as Toronto’s mayor on Monday night, defeating Brad Bradford by more than 127,000 votes.

Chow appears to have captured 54 per cent of the vote, with more than 99 per cent of all polls reporting.

Meanwhile, several other incumbent mayors elsewhere in the GTHA have been defeated.

The CP24-CTV Election Desk is projecting that city councillor Alvin Tedjo defeated incumbent Carolyn Parrish in the race for Mississauga’s mayor. In Hamilton, Keanin Loomis defeated Andrea Horwath, who finished a distant third.

  • Alvin Tedjo beats out Parrish and Crombie to become new mayor of Mississauga

items.body:
Air Canada flight crews who flew to several cities in Europe last week were relocated to secondary hotel locations due to civil unrest related to widespread protests, a source with knowledge on the situation confirmed with CTVNews.ca.

Air Canada crews arriving in Paris, Nice, Lyon, Nantes and Milan between Oct. 23 and 25 were sent to different locations to avoid potential disruption of crew rest.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The Air Canada Master Executive Council of the Air Line Pilots Association, Int’l (ALPA), said in an email to CTVNews.ca that they work closely with airline security teams and government contacts to monitor global threats and co-ordinate crew member safety during critical events.

“With safety as our top priority, relocations are common practice in the industry whenever there is a potential safety concern or possibility for disruption to our rest,” the email said.

It added that crews on layover are always told to follow the Canadian government’s travel advisory information.

Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson did not confirm the location change, but said in an email with CTVNews.ca that safety is always the airline’s top priority.

“As a global airline, we continuously monitor events worldwide, follow government guidance and conduct our own security assessments in consultation with industry partners,” he said in email. “When warranted, we may temporarily relocate crew accommodations closer to the airport to ensure the on-time operation of flights to Canada.”

Protest movement spread across Europe

Students in France began protesting school conditions last September. As the demonstrations grew in size, so did the issues that were being protested, including the cost of living. Protesters in Spain joined in shortly after, focusing on housing costs, along with Italy, Belgium, Albania, Austria, Greece, Ireland and Portugal.

Over the weekend, more than 400,000 people across France took to the streets, and nearly 1,000 people were arrested.

In Italy, hundreds of troops were sent in to monitor the protests in Rome, Milan and Turin, over the weekend. which were mostly peaceful.

Many luxury boutiques in Milan’s fashion district including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, boarded up their front windows to deter possible looters.

With files from rom CTV News’ Daniel Otis and The Associated Press.

items.title: PM Carney says ‘U.S. is coming closer to our position’ as trade talks gain momentum
items.description: Amid reporting by CTV News that trade talks between Canada and the U.S. are gaining momentum, Mark Carney said the Trump administration is 'coming closer to our position.'
items._ogDesc: Amid reporting by CTV News that trade talks between Canada and the U.S. are gaining momentum, Mark Carney said the Trump administration is 'coming closer to our position.'
items.body:
OTTAWA — Amid reporting by CTV News that trade talks between Canada and the U.S. are gaining momentum, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trump administration is “coming closer to our position.”

Carney made the comments during a question-and-answer period with reporters after a meeting between First Nation leaders and First Ministers in Ottawa on Monday.

Carney also said, however, he can’t guarantee U.S. President Donald Trump will respect anything they sign.

When talks broke down completely in August, Carney said during a speech referring to the U.S. administration that “sometimes its signature was written in pencil.”

Asked about those comments by CTV News deputy bureau chief Marieke Walsh on Monday, and specifically how he knows the U.S president will sign in pen, Carney said: “I don’t know that.”

“Canada’s ready to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians, all Canadians, with very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in in August,” Carney also said, when asked by Walsh whether he trusts the president.

“To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there’s a greater prospect of a deal,” he added. “But we’ll judge it and if there is something, we’ll judge it as a whole.”

CTV News reported on Sunday based on multiple government and industry sources that there is considerable appetite from the White House to ink a deal with Canada, in part because of Trump’s political vulnerabilities ahead of next week’s midterm elections.

One of the sources told CTV News the Americans appear to have shown more interest in reaching an agreement than they have “in all the weeks prior.”

With files from CTV News’ Marieke Walsh, Vassy Kapelos, Graham Richardson and Mike Le Couteur

items.title: PM Carney says it’s time to move beyond Indian Act
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will instruct his ministers to work with First Nations to move Canada beyond the Indian Act — which could mean reforming it or abolishing it altogether.
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will instruct his ministers to work with First Nations to move Canada beyond the Indian Act — which could mean reforming it or abolishing it altogether.
items.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will instruct his ministers to work with First Nations to move Canada beyond the Indian Act — which he said could mean reforming it or abolishing it altogether.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting with First Nations chiefs and premiers in Ottawa today, Carney said the elimination of the Indian Act has been sought by many First Nations leaders, including Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew.

Earlier in the day, Kinew told reporters during a break in the meeting that Canada needs a relationship between First Nations and the government “that reflects who Indigenous people are as Canadians.”

Carney said “moving beyond” the Indian Act could involve abolition or reform. But he said it would only happen in partnership with First Nations leadership.

“The suggestion of reforming, potentially abolishing and fully modernizing governance, is that a process, co-developed, needs to be put in place, and the federal government is open to that process,” Carney said.

Carney said the idea of abolishing or modernizing the Indian Act was discussed openly in the room.

“Not everybody, but other participants raised the desirability. So it’s already starting from the right place in that it’s not the federal government deciding something should be done. It’s responding to a request,” Carney said.

“I think this was the spirit of this meeting — certainly the spirit I took — the ability to sit down together and develop that co-development, gives me hope that we can we can finally move forward from this.”

The Indian Act has been in effect since 1876 to govern First Nations status in Canada. It has been amended several times to reflect changes in how status is conferred.

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said there are some protections in the act for First Nations, and First Nations should be able to decide how to move forward.

“Look, that’s a question that was just posed today in the room among First Nations. Some First Nations; others would be very reserved,” Woodhouse Nepinak.

“But there is, you know, a diversity of First Nations from coast to coast to coast, where in every province and territory in this beautiful country that we all share. And that question is going to be up to them to decide.”

Kinew said he feels the Indian Act should be abolished altogether. He held up his First Nations status card, which he said identifies him as an “Indian within the meaning of the Indian Act.”

“It’s time to abolish the Indian Act,” Kinew said. “It’s long overdue that we have a relationship with Indigenous Peoples in Canada that reflects who we are as Canadians today.”

Carney and most of the premiers sat down with chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations in Ottawa for a discussion Woodhouse Nepinak said is intended to help build prosperity for coming generations.

Monday’s closed-door meeting is the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities.

The Kelowna agreement was not implemented after the Conservative government under former prime minister Stephen Harper took office just a few months later.

This meeting comes as Carney’s government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights.

Jeronimo Kataquapit, who was protesting the major projects push outside the meeting venue in Ottawa, chided the federal government and the Assembly of First Nations over the lack of youth representation at the meeting.

“These major projects cannot move forward without our free, prior and informed consent, and it’s the youth that stand to be the most impacted by the decisions made today by all leadership, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous alike,” Kataquapit said from the sidewalk in front of the Diefenbaker Building.

Protester Katisha Paul, an advocate for youth and women, questioned the Assembly of First Nations’ mandate to negotiate on First Nations’ behalf.

“I’m not in that room today but I can imagine and speculate that the voices of our ancestors are not being heard, they’re not being voiced and they’re not being amplified because many of those elected band council chiefs have lost their ways,” Paul said.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025 when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.

First Nations leaders warned the compressed timelines would interfere with their rights and lead to court challenges. Provincial governments have enacted similar legislation.

But tensions are boiling over for a number of other reasons as well, including the lands claim process in British Columbia, the newly announced Pacific Link pipeline project in Alberta and development of the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in Ontario. In many cases, it’s youth who are pushing back on First Nations leaders, the premiers and prime minister.

Carney said Monday it’s “sobering” to consider that this is the first meeting to bring together federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in two decades.

“Our task is twofold. First is to work together to create opportunities for all our peoples, while building a country that is stronger, more sovereign and more independent,” he said.

“And secondly, our task is to live our values fully of a fair and inclusive Canada.”

While some First Nations are opposed to Carney’s development agenda and those of the provinces, others are open to the idea of increasing economic activity in their territories.

Nisga’a Nation President Eva Clayton told reporters ahead of the meeting she supports Carney’s plans and that she and other modern treaty holders are at the meeting to support Canada.

By Alessia Passafiume and Kyle Duggan

With files from Nick Murray

Correction

This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly referred to Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak as Grand Chief.

items._ogDesc: DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire Instacart in a deal that could value the grocery-delivery platform at about US$17 billion, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday.
items.body:
DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire Instacart in a deal that could value the grocery-delivery platform at about US$17 billion, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday.

A deal may be finalized as soon as Wednesday, although there are no guarantees it will come together, the person said. Instacart’s deal talks with Uber are no longer active, the person added.

Shares of Instacart, which had a market value of about US$13 billion as of Friday’s close, rose about eight per cent in regular trading, while DoorDash fell around six per cent.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the developments on Monday.

The food delivery industry has been grappling with rising labour costs, tighter regulation of delivery workers and growing competition after the pandemic-driven boom in online ordering faded.

The potential deal comes as delivery companies expand into grocery and retail to drive growth beyond restaurant delivery, with DoorDash buying Deliveroo and Uber acquiring Postmates and Delivery Hero.

If successful, the acquisition of Instacart would give DoorDash access to the platform’s established marketplace and retailer ties, which it could combine with its own vast delivery network and customer base.

The grocery platform has been exploring a possible sale and has held preliminary discussions with potential buyers including Uber and DoorDash, the Information reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.

Instacart declined to comment when contacted by Reuters, while Uber and DoorDash did not immediately respond.

“Strategically, DoorDash looks like the more natural fit for Instacart, given the complementary strengths of its restaurant delivery network and Instacart’s grocery expertise,” said Nick Smith, co-founder of growth strategy consultancy Manifesto Growth Architects.

“For Uber, the opportunity would be to deepen its position as an everyday convenience platform. But an acquisition only makes sense if it delivers incremental customer value and profitable growth — not simply greater scale.”

Separately, Instacart said in a regulatory filing on Monday it would wind down its Caper Cart smart shopping-cart business by the end of the second quarter of 2027, expecting pre-tax charges of US$55 million to US$80 million related to the move.

(Reporting by Sanskriti Shekhar and Anuja Bharat Mistry in Bengaluru; Editing by Shreya Biswas)

items._ogDesc: Days after launching its first folding iPhone, Apple acknowledged on Monday that some of the devices exhibit display problems and said it will replace them.
items.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — Days after launching its first folding iPhone, Apple acknowledged on Monday that some of the devices exhibit display problems and said it will replace them.

Apple started shipping the iPhone Duo last week, with customers around the world lining up for tight inventory after initial online orders sold out in minutes. Analysts have said Apple is likely to face supply constraints because the iPhone Duo, which unfolds like a passport booklet, is complex to manufacture.

Over the weekend, social media posts showed the iPhone Duo with cracks and lines in the inner display along the central hinge where the iPhone Duo folds.

Apple acknowledged the problems on Monday, saying affected units tend to show the problem quickly.

“We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units,” Apple said in a statement.

“If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement.“ Apple did not comment on what might cause the issue.

iFixit, a firm that publishes teardown reports of electronic devices along with guides on how to repair them, said it used teardown footage, patents and CT scans to construct a 3D simulation of the iPhone Duo hinge that it compared with the reported damage locations.

iFixit said its simulations found the reported damage clustered just below where a display cable runs under the screen near a central support bar. That bar might be failing to drop out of the screen’s way as the phone is folded, “creating a small stress hotspot near the reported break location,” the company said.

Apple did not immediately comment on iFixit’s findings, which also concluded that the iPhone Duo is the most repairable foldable phone that it has tested.

Francisco Jeronimo, a vice president at market research firm IDC, said Apple’s quick replacement offer was the “right first step” in responding to the problems.

“We all remember when Samsung experienced problems with the original Galaxy Fold in 2019, but it also showed that a fast and transparent response can contain the damage to a category,“ Jeronimo said.

(Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco and Aditya Soni Bengaluru; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

items._ogDesc: U.S. stocks rose amid shaky trading for financial markets worldwide, as AI stocks kept swinging and Brazilian stocks tumbled.
items.body:
NEW YORK — U.S. stocks rose Monday amid shaky trading for financial markets worldwide, as AI stocks kept swinging and Brazilian stocks tumbled.

The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and more than recovered its losses from last week, pulling within 1.8 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 146 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.8 per cent.

The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.4 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

But stocks elsewhere in the artificial-intelligence industry remained unsettled. They’ve been swerving on worries about whether their industry’s boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips.

Meta helps lead the swings

Meta Platforms bounced up and down after outlining plans to raise US$35 billion by selling stock to help pay for its AI investments. It also said it could raise another US$60 billion by selling shares of a new class of its stock once it begins trading. Meta’s stock initially dropped more than 2 per cent, but it quickly flipped to a gain and then pulled back to a loss of 1.9 per cent.

Meta said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have already indicated they may buy a total of US$5 billion of stock in its offering. Those are strong signals of interest from chip companies that stand to benefit from additional AI investments. But they also give fuel to critics of “circular financing” who say it raises the risk if AI isn’t as successful as expected.

One big company at the center of the AI boom, Anthropic, gave details Monday about how much money it’s losing as it prepares to sell its stock on the publicly traded U.S. market for the first time.

Worries remain about borrowing for AI

SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket company that also runs the xAI business, had similar swings after it announced a roughly US$40 billion deal with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management to lease AI computing power. Its stock initially fell nearly 2 per cent before flipping to a gain of 1.9 per cent and then finishing with a dip of 0.4 per cent.

Musk warned over the weekend that hundreds of companies that rent out AI computing power are under threat because of the difficulty in borrowing money, saying on his social-media platform, X, that they could face “guppy-level death and consolidation.”

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI computing power that it rents to customers over the cloud, has been at the center of investors’ worries in recent weeks. On Monday, it dropped 5.5 per cent quickly after trading began, only to flip to a gain of 6.6 per cent before moderating to a rise of 1.8 per cent. Such minute-to-minute swings have become commonplace for it in recent days.

All told, the S&P 500 rose 53.09 points to 7,676.77. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 146.42 to 52,361.58, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 214.04 to 26,169.38.

It’s a big week for profit reports

Profit reports from huge tech companies this week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going, and whether it’s producing the profits and productivity that proponents promised.

Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.

Companies across all industries are under pressure to report strong growth in their profits. Expectations for big growth are what allowed stock prices to run to records recently despite worries about high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns.

Verizon Communications fell 3.5 per cent even though it reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, as its revenue fell short of forecasts.

Roughly one out of every three stocks in the S&P 500 is scheduled to report its latest quarterly results this week.

Brazilian stocks tumble following mixed moves in other markets

In stock markets abroad, Brazilian stocks fell sharply after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection in a result that surprised investors.

The worry among investors is that he could increase the government’s spending and put more pressure on its debt. The Bovespa stock index in Brazil dropped 13.7 per cent.

Other governments around the world are also feeling pressure because of high debt loads and strained budgets, including the United States. France has been at the center of the worries recently following violent protests in the country.

  • Latest updates on international news here

But yields on French government bonds eased Monday, and its CAC 40 stock index rose 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s better moves. Indexes also rose in other European markets following a mixed finish in Asia.

The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will be meeting to vote on interest rates later this week.

Yields ease ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve’s meeting

In the U.S. bond market, yields fell for longer-term Treasurys. The yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.98 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Friday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month.

The two-year Treasury yield rose to 4.71 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Friday. It more closely tracks expectations for what the Federal Reserve will do with overnight interest rates, and the widespread expectation is that it will say on Wednesday that it is leaving the federal funds rate alone following its latest meeting.

The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, which has remained much higher than anyone would like.

Oil prices swing

The price for a barrel of Brent crude swung between gains and losses through the day before settling at US$110.74, down 0.9 per cent. It remains near the high end of its range since the war with Iran began. The highest price for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude since then is nearly US$120, reached in March.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Michelle Chapman and Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

TORONTO — Roots Corp. says Meghan Roach has stepped down as president and chief executive as its go-private transaction with Marquee Brands has closed.

Roach has been in the CEO role since 2020 after first joining the company as interim chief financial officer in 2019. 

The company says in a news release she will continue to serve in an advisory role to ensure a smooth leadership transition.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The go-private transaction was announced in August at a price of $4.10 per share and passed a shareholder vote earlier this month with more than 99 per cent support.

The company says Roots shares are now expected to be delisted “shortly” from the Toronto Stock Exchange.   

Marquee Brands also manages the Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli labels and intends to expand Roots to other markets like Korea, India and Mexico.

items.title: Banking fees are hard to see, predict and compare, FCAC review finds
items.description: A $2.45-billion fee pool and costly account switching put competitiveness in the spotlight
items.content: <p>A $2.45-billion fee pool and costly account switching put competitiveness in the spotlight</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639286467596574248.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A $2.45-billion fee pool and costly account switching put competitiveness in the spotlight
items.body:
Bank fees that look small one at a time can be hard to see, predict and compare, the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) said in a review released Friday. It added that the costs can add up over time, especially for lower-income Canadians.

The 130-page A Review of Banking Fees in Canada, requested by Ottawa in Budget 2025, looked at fees on personal deposit accounts, not mortgages. Across nine fee categories, financial institutions earned an estimated $2.45 billion in 2025, the Globe and Mail reported.

Where costs get hidden

FCAC said multiple fees can apply to a single transaction, foreign exchange and cross-border debit fees can be embedded in a purchase price, and usage-based fees are hard to predict when customers cannot track their transactions.

FCAC’s backgrounder also flagged multiple fees on one ATM withdrawal, excess transaction fees, and prepaid product fees that can erode balances over time. It said point-in-time disclosures do not always show cumulative costs.

The review said customers with lower incomes, less savings or heavier reliance on daily banking may be disproportionately affected, CBC reported.

“Canadians should be able to clearly understand what they are paying for banking services. When fees make the full cost harder to see, it affects both affordability and competition,” FCAC commissioner Shereen Benzvy Miller said in the release. “More transparency makes it easier for consumers to compare options and save money, and financial institutions have stronger incentives to compete for their business.”

Switching, competition and open banking

The review also pointed to barriers to switching. Transfer-out fees raise the cost of moving an account, and customers face indirect costs such as time and paperwork. “We need financial institutions to remove the friction for switching,” Benzvy Miller said in an interview with the Globe. Canada’s six largest banks together hold more than 90% of the market, the Globe reported.

FCAC said consumer-driven banking, also known as open banking, could make fees more visible and help consumers compare and switch providers. The Consumer-Driven Banking Act received royal assent in March. Proposed regulations published in June place the framework under the Bank of Canada’s oversight. It would let people share their financial data with accredited providers of their choice.

The mortgage industry has long advocated for open banking, CMP has reported.

The Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) did not directly address the findings in its response. CBA chief executive Anthony Ostler said in a statement: “When money is put in a bank in Canada, deposits are insured and the bank is overseen by regulators who ensure Canadians are treated fairly and their money is secure.”

What it means for brokers

The review does not examine mortgage products. But everyday banking costs shape clients’ monthly cash flow, and brokers who want to discuss total cost can point clients to FCAC’s Account Comparison Tool and the low-cost and no-cost account commitment the agency supervises.

Ontario’s financial services regulator has proposed refusing to renew the licence of mortgage agent Anna Angelidis, alleging her past conduct and false information on a licence application make her unsuitable to be licensed.

The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) announced the notice of proposal Friday. The allegations have not been proven. Angelidis has requested a hearing before the Financial Services Tribunal.

FSRA says Angelidis is not suitable to hold a licence under the Mortgage Brokerages, Lenders and Administrators Act, 2006 and its regulations. It alleges her past conduct gives reasonable grounds to believe she will not deal or trade in mortgages lawfully, honestly and with integrity. It also alleges she provided false information on a licence application.

The regulator’s announcement did not describe the conduct in question. It also did not say which licence level Angelidis holds, which brokerage authorized her, or when a hearing might take place.

Suitability under scrutiny

The case fits a broader push by FSRA to police who is fit to hold a licence. When it released its final licensing suitability guidance in July 2024, Huston Loke, FSRA’s executive vice-president of market conduct, said: “This is the first time we’re releasing guidance that explains how we assess if someone is suitable to hold a licence, strengthening sector practices and further protecting Ontarians working with mortgage professionals.”

FSRA’s guidance says the regulator may refuse, restrict, suspend or revoke a licence if it has reasonable grounds to believe someone is unsuitable. It also says oversight of agents and brokers is a brokerage’s ongoing responsibility.

Recent notices have turned on similar questions. In a December 2025 notice, FSRA alleged that a Level 2 agent answered “No” on a renewal application when asked whether he was under investigation. A March 2026 notice proposed refusing another agent’s renewal in a case FSRA framed as a test of suitability. Those cases are separate from Angelidis’s, and the hearing requests in each remain unresolved.

What happens next

A notice of proposal is not a final decision. In a 2025 case, CMP reported that FSRA may proceed with its proposed order if no hearing is requested within 15 days of receipt. Because Angelidis requested one, the Tribunal will review the proposal.

For brokers and principal brokers, the case is a reminder that FSRA can assess suitability at renewal, and that the accuracy of what is submitted on licensing forms is part of that assessment. Brokerages may want to confirm that their screening and supervision processes match FSRA’s published expectations.

items.title: Oxford Economics sees Bank of Canada hikes arriving a year early
items.description: Oil-driven inflation, a weakening job market and fragile housing complicate brokers’ rate outlook
items.content: <p>Oil-driven inflation, a weakening job market and fragile housing complicate brokers’ rate outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639286463485125643.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Oil-driven inflation, a weakening job market and fragile housing complicate brokers’ rate outlook
items.body:
Oxford Economics now expects the Bank of Canada to raise its key rate by a cumulative 50 basis points by January 2027, about a year earlier than it projected in September, as surging oil prices push inflation higher.

The forecast lands days before the central bank’s Oct. 28 decision, with the overnight rate at 2.25%. Oxford expects 25-basis-point hikes on Oct. 28 and in December, returning the rate to what it estimates is a neutral 2.75%. It does not view the moves as “the start of a tightening cycle.”

Markets have moved toward a hike. A Reuters poll of economists conducted Oct. 21-23 found 19 of 34 (56%) expect a quarter-point increase to 2.50% next week and another by the end of March. Overnight swaps implied about a 75% chance of an October hike, according to Bloomberg data.

Oil lifts headline inflation, not yet core

Consumer prices rose 3.1% year over year in September, up from 3.0% in August, with gasoline up 27.8%, CMP reported. The Bank’s preferred core measures, CPI-trim and CPI-median, averaged 1.9%.

Oxford expects headline inflation in the mid-3% range in late 2026 and early 2027. It assumes Brent crude stays above US$100 a barrel for the next six months. Oil hit $117 a barrel on Oct. 23, Reuters reported.

Governor Tiff Macklem has grown more wary. Speaking at IMF meetings in Bangkok, he warned that “the risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent has gone up,” RBC economist Abbey Xu noted.

Others see less urgency. Dominion Lending Centres chief economist Sherry Cooper said last week: “Today’s inflation report reinforces our view that higher gasoline prices temporarily boost headline inflation while further eroding household purchasing power. However, these energy-driven increases, largely tied to geopolitical tensions, are unlikely to trigger a broader resurgence in underlying inflation.”

Oxford, too, expects slack and slower shelter inflation to keep core inflation from rising sharply. Still, it called the October decision “a toss-up” after softer jobs and inflation data, adding: “even if it doesn’t hike in October, we still anticipate it’ll lift the overnight rate by a cumulative 50bps by January.”

Housing and household debt in focus

Statistics Canada said the economy lost 68,000 jobs in September, lifting unemployment to 6.5%. Oxford trimmed its 2027 GDP growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 1.3% and left 2026 at 1.0%. It projects the 10-year government bond yield near 4% through 2027, a key input for fixed mortgage pricing.

On housing, the report said: “We expect home sales volumes and prices to slide this fall and into early next year as mortgage rates rise.” It added that elevated debt “will continue to constrain spending by Canadian households and make them vulnerable to job losses, higher interest rates, and a resurgence in oil prices.”

Trade remains a drag. The US imposed 50% tariffs on C$27.6 billion of Canadian goods effective Aug. 22, and Canada countered from Sept. 8, according to a Finance Canada statement.

Oxford warned that if oil prices don’t ease in 2027, the Bank could “hike rates to the top of its neutral range at 3.25%, or even higher into restrictive territory.”

For brokers, the Bank will release updated inflation projections alongside the decision. Variable-rate clients feel any hike through prime, while renewals face fixed pricing set by bond yields. Both groups may need early conversations about payment tolerance and rate holds.

items.title: PBO cuts 2026 growth forecast to 0.9% as new tariffs weigh on economy
items.description: Mortgage renewals, a softer job market and the Nov. 5 budget loom over a cautious outlook
items.content: <p>Mortgage renewals, a softer job market and the Nov. 5 budget loom over a cautious outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639286460879095360.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage renewals, a softer job market and the Nov. 5 budget loom over a cautious outlook
items.body:
Parliament’s budget watchdog has cut its 2026 growth forecast to 0.9% and projects federal deficits above $63 billion through 2030-31, citing a new round of US tariffs and Canadian countermeasures.

The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) released its Economic and Fiscal Outlook last week. It now sees real GDP growth of 1.5% in 2027, down from 1.1% for 2026 and 1.6% for 2027 in June. The PBO estimates that trade measures in place since early 2025 could shrink the economy by about 1.4% over the medium term if they become permanent.

“Canada faces a more challenging economic and fiscal outlook than we projected in June,” parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan said. “Additional trade measures and ongoing uncertainty are weighing on growth in real output – what we produce as a country.”

Jobs, inflation and the rate path

The PBO expects unemployment to rise to 6.7% by the end of 2026 as employment falls faster than the labour force. Its figures predate Statistics Canada’s September report, which showed 68,000 jobs lost and unemployment at 6.5%.

Inflation should average 2.8% in 2026, driven by higher energy prices tied to disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and by pressure from Canada’s countermeasures.

The PBO assumes the Bank of Canada starts raising its policy rate early in 2027 and reaches a neutral 2.75% by mid-year. It stressed this is a projection assumption, not advice on monetary policy. Markets are pricing in something sooner. A Reuters poll found 19 of 34 economists expect a quarter-point hike on Oct. 28.

For households, the PBO flagged that consumption could prove weaker than projected as those “renewing mortgages taken out when interest rates were lower face higher payments, leaving less income for other spending.” It also expects residential investment to recover from a 2026 decline, helped by new federal housing measures and borrowing costs well below their 2023-24 peak.

Deficits and the Nov. 5 budget

The PBO projects a $63.3-billion deficit in 2026-27, down from $71.8 billion in its June outlook. It then sees the shortfall peaking at $70.2 billion in 2027-28 and easing to $67.8 billion by 2030-31. New measures, including $36 billion for the Productivity Mega Deduction and $7.5 billion in tariff support, cost $52.6 billion over five years. That more than offsets $37.4 billion in additional fiscal room from stronger revenues.

Public debt charges are the fastest-growing federal expense, rising from $59.3 billion in 2026-27 to $83.0 billion by 2030-31. Federal debt per person is projected to climb from $33,436 to $39,191 over the same period. A permanent 100-basis-point rise in rates would add $5.1 billion to debt charges in the first year.

The PBO expects Ottawa to meet its operating-balance anchor in 2028-29, but not its goal of a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio. “A balanced operating budget anchor should not be interpreted as a balanced fiscal position,” Ryan said. “By design, it excludes debt-financed capital spending, meaning borrowing and debt can continue to grow while the target is being achieved.”

Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne said the budget, due Nov. 5, will “outline the next steps in our plan to build a stronger, more resilient and more affordable Canada,” The Canadian Press reported. The PBO’s numbers do not include measures from that budget. It judges risks to its outlook as roughly balanced, with trade policy the dominant uncertainty.

For brokers, the report is a prompt to revisit renewal scenarios with clients, particularly those in trade-exposed work, before the Bank’s decision and the budget land.

items.title: Sutton Group Announces Strategic Partnership With Ace Project Marketing
items.description:
Led by entrepreneur Ross McCredie, Vancouver-based Sutton Group has announced that they are partnering with Kelowna-based Ace Project Marketing, the latest move by the McCredie-led real estate company as it continues to expand its horizons.

The partnership will see Ace’s project marketing expertise and experience working with developers join forces with Sutton’s national network of over 6,000 agents in a way that the two say will benefit developers, real estate agents, and homebuyers.

As part of the partnership, Ace Project Marketing will be launching Ace Everywhere, a project marketing program designed exclusively for Sutton Group’s agents.

The firms said in a press release that the "program combines Ace’s centralized strategy, marketing and production capabilities with local agents’ market knowledge, relationships and licensed sales expertise.”

The result is Sutton agents will have support to work with presales, and Ace will bring its expertise to new markets across the country.

“For developers, the partnership brings together Ace’s insights into purchaser expectations and its sales and marketing expertise with Sutton’s national reach,” the companies said. “This collaboration offers a trusted sales and marketing pipeline, helping developers connect their projects with prospective buyers and the agents who advise them. By streamlining projects and maximizing presale success rates, the partnership supports market-driven developments and long-term success.”

“Combining Sutton’s national network of 6,000 agents with Ace’s customized market intelligence and project marketing expertise allows us to deliver data-driven solutions grounded in a people-first approach,” said Ace CEO Chad MacTavish. “Ace Everywhere gives us a practical way to grow alongside Sutton’s agents, combining the strength of a national platform with the local expertise every development needs. It reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity for Canadian housing and our commitment to building the capabilities to support it.”

Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie (left) and Ace Project Marketing CEO Chad MacTavish (right).

The Sutton Group team and Ace Project Marketing team.

“This partnership with Ace combines Sutton’s deep local roots across Canada with expertise in new housing, exactly when it’s needed most,” added Sutton Group President James Innis. “With new-home construction starts and preconstruction sales facing significant headwinds, we’re helping shape much-needed housing solutions that reflect the needs of each community, and giving our agents new ways to support buyers through a changing market.”

Sutton Group

Commenting on the partnership, Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie called it “an exciting step forward in enhancing the services within Canadian real estate” and part of the company’s “technology-driven approach” towards delivering unparalleled value and homeowner-focused solutions for Canadians.

Sutton Group has taken several steps forward in recent years, after McCredie — through McCredie Investments — acquired the company in 2023. McCredie has spent the past few years positioning the company for long-term success in a technology-driven world and pushing the company towards a wealth-management model.

Those moves include the November 2025 acquisition of Ottawa-based real estate data technology company Homicity. With the acquisition, Homicity Co-Founder and CEO Jamie Blades joined Sutton Group as VP of Technology & Partner Success.

This spring, the company then announced a partnership with American luxury real estate brokerage Elliman (formerly known as Douglas Elliman) that would see the two companies create a new two-way referral program for their agents.

That same month, Sutton Group also announced that myAbode — an AI-driven deal processing “operating system” for residential brokerages — was making a strategic investment in Sutton Group and providing its brokerage optimization technology to Sutton’s agents.

Sutton Group has also continued to expand its footprint, opening new offices in Surrey, West Vancouver, Kelowna, Calgary, Stratford, and Gatineau-Ottawa over the past 12 months.

items.description:

The post Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: A Bank of Canada staff paper finds about 80% of the building boost from rate cuts comes from excess demand, and ignoring shelter inflation fuels booms.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate industry often argues the central bank should ignore shelter inflation and keep rates low to boost supply. A new Bank of Canada (BoC) staff paper tests both claims, and neither holds up as a blanket rule. The researchers find that ignoring shelter inflation during a demand-driven boom is destabilizing to the economy and pushes valuations higher. While rate cuts get more homes built, roughly 80% of that comes from excess demand created by monetary stimulus.

Housing FOMO Makes Ignoring Shelter Inflation Risky

Can the central bank safely ignore shelter inflation? Not when demand is driving it, according to the researchers. “Monetary policy should not look through shelter inflation when it is driven by housing demand shocks. Looking through creates a more volatile economy especially when faced with extrapolative expectations,” they explain.

Extrapolative expectations is a $10 term ($184.70 in 2026 dollars) for assuming a trend will continue. Home prices rise because that’s just what they do—so buyers who believe that load up on more housing and debt during a boom.

The researchers modelled a boom where home prices climb 20% over two years. Excluding shelter inflation from policy decisions pushes overvaluation as much as 2.2 percentage points higher than a policy that includes it. When buyers have rational expectations, the gap peaks around 1.3 points. In other words, trend-chasing led to a 70% larger overshoot.

“This amplifies financial stability risks, especially when price dynamics are partly driven by past increases in house prices,” warn the researchers.

Rate Cuts Are Steroids For Demand, Not A Supply Fix

Factoring shelter into rate decisions during a boom makes a hike more likely. Higher rates cool demand over time, but they immediately raise financing costs for homebuilders. Cheaper money means more building, argues the industry. In isolation, the math makes sense. Reality is a little more complicated.

“While financing costs do affect housing supply, supply-side cost effects remain quantitatively secondary to demand-driven mechanisms operating through house prices and expectations,” explain the researchers.

They modelled a 100 basis point (bp) rate cut, which lifts residential investment 6.2%. Cheaper financing accounted for just 1.4 points of that, roughly 20%. The other 80% injection comes from excess housing demand. Rate cuts technically get more homes built, but primarily by incentivizing more housing consumption.

Mortgage Interest Makes Rate Cuts Look Like Lower Inflation

After a rate cut, shelter inflation falls for about two years. That drop is mostly mechanical, as Canada includes mortgage interest costs (MIC) in CPI. Cheaper borrowing directly lowers measured shelter inflation, even though the real impact of monetary policy decisions isn’t fully reflected for 18 to 24 months. It’s a problem most countries avoid, including the United States.

Since CPI drives rate decisions and rates drive mortgage interest costs, mortgage interest creates a feedback loop. Rates fall, mortgage interest falls, measured inflation falls, and the BoC cuts rates to lift inflation back to target. The researchers call it a “policy amplification loop,” where easing reinforces the housing boom. It makes the case for ignoring mortgage interest, even as they warn against ignoring demand-driven shelter inflation.

We’ve covered this problem in depth before, so it’s nice to see it get some time in the monetary policy spotlight.

Hiking Rates Into A Supply Shock Slows Output, Not Inflation

When a supply crunch is driving shelter inflation, hiking rates barely makes a dent. Higher rates raise mortgage interest costs, offsetting much of the cooling in home prices.

Rents rise too. In the model, rental returns have to compete with what investors could earn on financial assets, so higher rates push rents up.

Responding to shelter with hikes “does little to reduce cumulative shelter inflation,” note the researchers. Total headline inflation ends up nearly identical whether the BoC reacts to shelter or not, according to the model. Economic output is a different story.

“In contrast, reacting to the housing supply shock leads to a significantly larger decline in output. This trade-off suggests that looking through housing supply shocks may be welfare-enhancing,” the researchers conclude.

Even the case for looking through shelter inflation comes with a caveat. They warn that if the supply shock persists, the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations rises, urging caution.

What The Bank of Canada’s Model Misses About Rates & Productivity

The researchers are clear: the BoC can’t safely ignore shelter inflation when demand is driving it, and rate cuts aren’t a supply strategy. Hikes restrain home prices even in a shortage, but measured shelter inflation barely moves, since higher mortgage interest costs and rents offset the cooling.

What the model doesn’t show is the cost to the rest of the economy. The study shows a 100 bp rate cut lifts residential investment 6.2%, dwarfing the boost to output and business investment. In this scenario of a housing demand shock, residential investment growth significantly outpaces the boost to business investment and economic output. The model treats this as a passing problem: one shock, and everything returns to normal within five years. That’s not reality.

The BoC doesn’t cut rates once, then take a decade off. Repeated easing has pushed residential investment’s growth past the rest of the economy, concentrating capital in housing. The model has no way for business investment to lift future productivity, the exact problem that policymakers are currently struggling with. It can’t count what’s lost when that capital is diverted from other industries, nor does it measure whether, when or how it returns. The paper shows where the stimulus goes. It just doesn’t capture the full cost.

items.title: BoC preview: What to expect from Wednesday's huge decision
items.description: Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move
items.content: <p>Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286370231956432.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move
items.body:
The Bank of Canada’s penultimate interest rate decision of 2026 arrives on Wednesday (October 28), and there's no consensus among experts on whether a rate hold or hike is in store.

The central bank has kept rates unchanged for nearly 12 months, with its last move in either direction arriving almost a year to the day of Wednesday’s announcement – a 25-basis-point cut on October 29, 2025.

The BoC’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable mortgage rates in Canada, has held steady since then as decisionmakers adopted a cautious approach during tense times marked by global economic uncertainty, a worsening trade dispute with the US, and inflation fears sparked by the US-Iran war.

Is a hike in store on Wednesday?

The Bank is at an “inflection point” as its next decision looms, according to Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) Economics, whose economists now say a quarter-point hike is the likeliest outcome from Wednesday’s meeting.

Still, that’s by no means a surefire thing. RBC’s Frances Donald (chief economist) and Nathan Janzen (assistant chief economist) see an almost equal probability that the BoC will hold steady this month but signal a rate hike on the way in December or January.

 Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge, meanwhile, doesn’t expect a hike between now and the end of the year – but said he anticipates the BoC will begin raising interest rates at some point in 2027, potentially in the spring.

But 19 of 34 economists polled by Reuters last week see a central bank rate jump to 2.50% on Wednesday, with a majority also pencilling in a further increase before March.

The main reason for the sudden prospect of a rate hike is concern about the national inflation outlook. The consumer price index (CPI) ticked higher last month, hitting 3.1% as surging fuel prices pushed prices higher.

However, observers including National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéfane Marion believe that increase was milder than might have been expected – strengthening the case for a further rate hold.

“Core inflation is still at 2%,” Marion said during an address at last week’s Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary. “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking [on October 28] and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

What the BoC decision will mean for mortgages

If the Bank increases rates on Wednesday, variable mortgage rates would also move higher because banks typically raise their prime rate in line with BoC moves.

Much attention will focus on the language used by BoC governor Tiff Macklem in his press conference after the announcement, with financial markets keeping a close eye on whether Macklem indicates rate increases are likely in the coming months.

As for the possible impact on the housing market of Wednesday’s decision?

A rate hold probably wouldn’t move the needle for national homebuying, which has remained sluggish through 2026 because of economic uncertainty and rising rates.

It’s unclear whether a rate hike would slow the market further, although activity has remained moribund as potential buyers stay on the sidelines even with rate increases on the horizon.

“You’d expect with lots of chatter about rate increases in Canada online bubbling through communities – plus the recent significant rise in fixed-rate mortgages in the United States – that there’d be some pull-ahead in activity,” Royal LePage president and chief executive officer Phil Soper told CMP earlier this month.

“You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs. Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat.”

items.description: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items._ogDesc: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items.body:
Uniqlo will open its first downtown Vancouver store at CF Pacific Centre in spring 2027, marking the Japanese clothing retailer’s seventh location in B.C.

The Japanese retailer will join the new Aritzia and Simons flagships to take up the space formerly occupied by Nordstrom. The three stores are scheduled to open between 2027 and 2028.

“We are incredibly proud to support the growth of Uniqlo, Simons and Aritzia across Canada with these premier locations at CF Pacific Centre,” said Lillian Tummonds, senior vice-president of retail at Cadillac Fairview, which owns and operates the shopping centre, in a statement.

“This major transformation reflects our shared commitment to creating unparalleled retail destinations, and we look forward to the energy and excitement these powerhouse brands will bring to the heart of downtown Vancouver.”

Bruce Winder, a retail analyst, said the development is a "continued vote" in downtown Vancouver retail space.

"Downtown Vancouver has had a bit of a hard time getting tenants. Recently, it's been a bit of a tough sell for some brands to sign leases," Winder said.

"And they've had to deal with ... the exit of Nordstrom. Not specifically in [Pacific Centre], but Saks Fifth Avenue have left, going back, Sears left, etc. So it's been tough to fill these large boxes."

In November 2025, Vancouver-based fashion retailer Aritzia announced plans for a four-level, 40,000-square-foot flagship boutique at CF Pacific Centre, with an opening initially targeted for 2027. Cadillac Fairview's latest announcement tentatively puts the opening in 2028.

Earlier this year, Quebec-based retailer Simons announced plans to open its first downtown Vancouver store at the shopping centre. The approximately 92,000-square-foot location will span three floors and is scheduled to open in fall 2027.

Winder said several mid-sized brands have been taking up space previously occupied by a single large retailer in downtowns across Canada, including Vancouver.

Another trend he has observed in B.C. is the rise of Asian retailers as some American chains, including Target and Nordstrom, have exited Canada, alongside the closure of Saks Off Fifth stores.

"U.S. companies seem to have a harder track record, where some of the other retailers from Asia, like Uniqlo, Miniso, Muji, and some other ones, have done better in Canada," he said.

Uniqlo opened its first Canadian store at CF Toronto Eaton Centre in 2016, followed by its first B.C. location at Metropolis at Metrotown in Burnaby in 2017.

items._ogDesc: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items.body:
Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.

Financial market odds for a rate hike were just over 83 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. The central bank's planned interest rate announcement on Wednesday will also include an updated monetary policy report.

The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent for seven consecutive meetings.

RBC economists said in a note to clients Thursday that they are now expecting a quarter-point hike as the central bank faces a “pivotal decision amid evolving economic conditions.”

Last week, Statistics Canada reported the annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as the war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices. Excluding gasoline, the consumer price index rose 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September, easing from 2.4 per cent in August, suggesting higher energy prices haven't significantly spread throughout the economy yet.

Meanwhile, jobs data from StatCan released earlier this month showed the labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September as the economy lost 68,000 positions.

However, the RBC economists said they have “very low conviction” on a rate hike happening this week, and see a significant chance the Bank of Canada instead uses the meeting to set up a hike in December or January.

"While we don’t see an immediate need for the BoC to hike now, at the same time, a 25-basis-point increase in the overnight rate on Wednesday won’t materially change our medium-term economic outlook compared to a December or January hike," the note reads.

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said in an interview that recent comments from Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem appeared to drive the change in expectations.

While speaking from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Macklem warned that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the inflation outlook at home.

“That essentially just emphasized that the central bank is increasingly worried about the potential impact of higher oil prices on future, broader inflation pressures, and they feel confident enough the economic backdrop is going to gradually continue to improve,” Janzen said.

The Bank of Canada released its latest business outlook survey last week, which suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter. However, it found that concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.

"All the economic data that we've had to date is consistent with the view that the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was getting closer to raising interest rates," Janzen said.

Canadian interest rates are still relatively low, he added, and the neutral range — where rates are neither helping nor hurting the economy — sits between 2.25 per cent and 3.25 per cent.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao said in an interview that it is clear the Bank of Canada is becoming more concerned about the persistence of rising energy prices, "and that's what's starting to change the calculus."

While a hike is likely, he said there are also arguments for the bank to hold its key rate.

"There's interest-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing, that are already dealing with higher bond yields and too much additional tightening risks some unnecessary weaker demand in that space," Ercolao said.

"Overall, Canada's economy is growing, but it's not necessarily overheating by any means."

The impact of U.S. trade tensions on overall investment and a weakening labour market also support a decision to hold interest rates, he said.

He said a hike on Wednesday would be a risk management measure to prevent the inflation shock from becoming more persistent.

Ercolao said higher energy prices are a double-edged sword for the domestic economy.

"On one hand, higher energy prices are good for producers and government, and corporate revenue intake. It creates higher incomes especially in commodity-producing provinces," he said.

"But at the same time, it's households especially that feel the pinch immediately from higher gasoline costs and then secondary to that, higher refined product costs end up feeding through the supply chain and into our end-user purchases."

Ercolao said that Canada has navigated the trade dispute "fairly well" by diversifying trade in certain sectors, including shipments of energy products to Asia and Europe.

"That said, there's still that acute pressure that's being placed on very reliant industries in Canada on the U.S., especially in Central Canada like Ontario and Quebec with our steel industry, our aluminum industry and our auto industry," he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: Some Canadian homebuyers tune out tariff noise as trade war rumbles on
items.description: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.content: <p>Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286291616924369.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.body:
Geopolitical chaos and global economic uncertainty have stretched into 2026, pushing a hoped-for Canadian housing market recovery even further down the line as potential homebuyers wait for a calmer environment to emerge before making their move.

Bond market unease has sent five-year Government of Canada yields higher in recent months, pushing fixed mortgage rates upwards, while speculation is growing about at least one potential Bank of Canada rate hike in the months ahead.

Would-be buyers are still keeping a close eye on the latest political news – but while the announcement of US tariffs at the beginning of last year sent shockwaves around bond markets and hugely dented homebuyer confidence, a degree of acceptance has set in among mortgage shoppers about the trade war.

That’s according to Ottawa-based Smart Debt Mortgages broker Chris Allard (pictured top), who told Canadian Mortgage Professional many clients were still determined to push ahead with their purchase plans even with no end to the trade dispute in sight.

“I get the perception that people have largely tried to tune out some of the news and keep a positive mindset,” he said. “But there’s no doubt that everyone’s aware of what’s happening, and they’re aware that rates are rising and there’s significant concern for that.

“Now, the commentary that I often hear from borrowers, and this is true, is we see when Trump speaks now, the markets don’t automatically go up or automatically go down right away. And so that translates into the conversation that we’re having with our clients because they’re now recognizing that maybe it’s just a bunch of noise.”

Borrowers are still cognizant of the impact a big, unexpected development in the trade war would have for the economy and their plans – but they’re equally focused on making their mortgage work and optimizing their financial picture to move forward with their deal, Allard said.

“They’re trying to just look at their personal budget and try to make an educated decision based on the current environment rather than predicting if home values are up or down or rates are up or down,” he said. “They’re going, ‘What are my payments now? Am I comfortable now? And do I have a safety net?’”

BoC rate not expected to surge, even if a hike is on the way

Opinion is divided among leading economists on what’s in store from the Bank of Canada’s decision this Wednesday. Experts including Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge don’t see a hike on the way yet, although Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) now marginally expects a 25-basis-point jump.

Most of the country’s top banks expect rate hikes to arrive at some point over the next year – but none are predicting the Bank of Canada’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable mortgage rates, will hit the highs seen in 2023-24.

That’s welcome news for borrowers, according to Allard. “I think a lot of Canadians might be surprised that the banks are not projecting significant prime rate increases,” he said. “It turns out that we did see fixed rate increases – and now it looks as though there won’t be significant prime rate increases.

“So I believe that just means that we might have more clients going into variable once they start to understand that dynamic.”

Clients focus on variable amid fixed-rate rises

Allard said he’s recently noted an increase in clientele wanting variable rates with a static payment amid a wider move away from fixed rates. “Bank of Montreal [BMO] offers that, TD Bank offers that, there’s a few others that offer it,” he said.

“Borrowers are [saying] ‘Well, maybe I can benefit from a rate in the high threes, have a stable payment, even though I’m taking a variable-rate product.’ It’s a really interesting move that we’re seeing from a consumer behaviour standpoint.”

items.title: District Energy Wants The Mechanical Room (And To Give Your Rooftop Back)
items.description:
Every residential tower gives up part of itself to equipment. From early plans, mechanical systems typically claim a room in the basement and a penthouse on the roof (the latter being prime real estate, mind you). This approach means that square footage is spoken for before the first suite is laid out.

Developers pay to build that space, but can’t sell or rent it. And today, with construction costs high and interest rate hikes back on the table, that cost is increasingly difficult to absorb.

“For developers building today, trying to make their projects pencil, taking capital off of traditional real estate development is a major factor,” said Diego Mandelbaum, Chief Development Officer at Corix, which builds and runs district energy systems as a utility across North America. “Reducing square footage for inefficient, building-scale mechanical space is a major piece of that, because doing so translates into both more usable area, and cost savings for developers.”

District energy moves thermal equipment out of individual buildings. In short: a central plant, usually located somewhere on, near, or below a project site, produces heat and chilled water for cooling and sends it through a network of pipes to every building connected to it, so the buildings themselves don’t need their own boilers. And because all of that energy is made in one place, the plant can switch to cleaner sources over time, like waste heat captured from a nearby power plant or wood waste that would otherwise go to landfill. This type of system has been around for well over a century — Corix’s district energy network at Ohio’s Cleveland Thermal dates back to 1894, for example — and now, the same central-plant model is helping today’s developers get space and capital back.

And those capital gains aren’t only about reclaimed square footage. Sometimes, they’re connected to meeting standards that are as well-meaning as they are costly. The starting point for the district energy system co-developed by Corix at Oakridge Park in Vancouver was a municipal low-carbon building policy. Meeting it tower by tower would have been an expensive effort — both in space and in capital. But that wasn’t the only way.

“At Oakridge Park, our solution was to rip out the mechanical equipment from each individual tower and centralize it. That allowed the development to meet the City’s green zoning requirements while saving a tremendous amount of capital and space,” Mandelbaum explained. At buildout, Oakridge Park will reach about 5 million square feet.

Oakridge Park (via Corix)

The savings can reach a project’s financing, too. CMHC is the only provider of mortgage loan insurance for multi-unit residential properties in Canada, and much of the country’s new rental housing is financed through it. And, CMHC-insured loans carry efficiency and sustainability requirements that are expensive to meet when approached one building at a time.

“We’re able to help developers meet these standards,” Mandelbaum says. In so many words, Corix can unlock financing solutions on a developer’s behalf, clearing a path to the CMHC-insured loans a project needs.

The earlier Corix is brought into a project, the more of those savings there are to find, since the team can help shape a master plan’s massing before plant spaces and penthouses get locked in. But no matter when the partnership is formed, the developer doesn’t carry the cost of the plant and pipes; Corix does, recovering that investment over the long term through the rates its customers pay for energy.

That means keeping those rates competitive comes first, and building too much, too soon would push them up. Which puts the pressure on timing.

“District energy doesn’t really work by just looking at an engineering study and asking, 'Can we make it work?' It’s about figuring out how to phase in your generation, and your capital, lock-in-step with the development," Mandelbaum said. "It's also about understanding that a developer will never give you certainty on how long it’ll take to build things out, because the market will never give you certainty."

So Corix builds in phases, leaning on modular construction and prefabrication to add capacity as buildings come online. At UniverCity, the residential community beside Simon Fraser University (SFU), work started with modular natural gas boilers while the community grew. Once the system had enough load, made possible by connecting SFU’s Burnaby campus, Corix invested in a much larger biomass plant, which burns wood waste otherwise bound for landfill. Today, the system heats the university and its neighbours, spanning nearly 5 million square feet in total.

Burnaby Mountain District Energy Utility near Simon Fraser University (via Corix)

Utah City, a sprawling master plan south of the border, is following the same path. There, Corix came into the picture after the first building was already up. Waiting on the grid wasn’t really an option: the development would have needed about 70 megawatts of power for its thermal systems, Mandelbaum explained, and the local utility would have needed 10 years to supply it.

Understandably, the developer had some questions about implementing district energy. But with construction in progress, the development team had tangible, tendered prices for mechanical equipment in hand, and could check Corix’s numbers against them directly. Spoiler: they held up.

“We built a modular plant in Washington state, we put it on a truck bed, we got it to site as soon as possible, and we got things energized within two years of the handshake,” Mandelbaum said.

Today, about 20 million square feet of real estate is set to be served by the system. Once enough of it is connected, Utah will see its own version of SFU’s switch: Corix will capture waste heat from a ~1.3-gigawatt gas-fired power plant about a mile away, which currently vents that heat into the atmosphere.

“What we're doing is closing the loop on what’s otherwise a wasted resource,” Mandelbaum explained.

Developments like these can take decades to build out, but Corix can handle a waiting game, thanks in large part to its ownership structure. The company is wholly owned by British Columbia Investment Management Corporation, which manages public pensions in British Columbia.

“We’re able to take a very long-term view," Mandelbaum said. "We have patient capital."

Utah City (via Corix)

That long view extends to everyone a system touches. Before a shovel goes in the ground, Corix looks at each project from every stakeholder’s side: the developer, the regulator, the municipality and, ultimately, the customer.

For Mandelbaum, the approach comes down to one question: “How’s a customer going to feel and experience this?”

And for the people who’ll call these communities home, the payoff lives in space reclaimed at the lower level, or on the sun-soaked rooftop.

“Just imagine," Mandelbaum said, "if every single rooftop was able to be used for amenity space. Or for recreation. Or for a garden."
